title: PCR Workflow: Conventional & Real-Time RT-PCR

references.label: CLSI Standards for Clinical Laboratory Practice

purpose: To detect and, for real-time methods, quantify specific nucleic acid targets by exponentially amplifying a defined DNA (or reverse-transcribed RNA) segment, enabling detection of pathogens or genetic targets present at very low starting quantities.
principle: PCR cycles through denaturation (separating double-stranded DNA), annealing (primers bind their complementary target sequence), and extension (a thermostable DNA polymerase synthesizes a new complementary strand), doubling the target sequence with each cycle in principle, so even a small number of starting copies becomes readily detectable after enough cycles. RT-PCR first reverse-transcribes an RNA target into complementary DNA before amplification, extending the same principle to RNA targets (e.g. many RNA viruses). Real-time (quantitative) PCR adds a fluorescent reporter system that produces a signal proportional to amplified product after each cycle, allowing both detection and, via the cycle number at which signal crosses a threshold, an estimate of the starting target quantity — a fundamentally different readout than the end-point gel visualization used in conventional PCR.
requiredMaterials: Thermal cycler (conventional) or real-time PCR instrument
Dedicated, physically separated pre- and post-amplification work areas
requiredReagents: Extracted nucleic acid template (see the related DNA/RNA extraction step)
Primers specific to the target sequence
Thermostable DNA polymerase and reaction buffer/dNTPs

procedure.instruction: Extract nucleic acid from the specimen using a validated method appropriate to the sample type and target (DNA or RNA).

procedure.note: Physical separation of pre- and post-amplification workflows, and unidirectional workflow, is a core molecular contamination-control principle, not an optional convenience.
procedure.instruction: Prepare the PCR reaction mix (primers, polymerase, buffer, and reverse transcriptase if amplifying RNA) in a physically separate pre-amplification area to minimize contamination risk.
Add template to the reaction mix, including required positive and no-template negative controls in the same run.
Run the thermal cycling program (denaturation, annealing, extension, repeated for the specified number of cycles) specific to the primer set and target.

For conventional PCR, visualize the amplified product by gel electrophoresis and compare band size/presence against expected controls. For real-time PCR, monitor the fluorescence signal each cycle and determine the cycle threshold (Ct) for the sample relative to controls/standards.

procedure.note: Never interpret a patient result from a run whose controls failed — the run must be repeated.
procedure.instruction: Interpret the result only after confirming that both the positive and no-template negative controls performed as expected — an invalid control set invalidates the run regardless of the patient sample result.

observations: For conventional PCR, record band presence/size on gel electrophoresis. For real-time PCR, record Ct value and amplification curve shape relative to controls.
interpretation: Detection of the target sequence indicates its presence in the extracted template; a Ct value reflects relative starting quantity but is method/assay-specific and not directly comparable across different assay platforms without validated correlation.
precautions: Strict unidirectional workflow (extraction → reaction setup → amplification → detection) and physically separate areas/equipment for pre- and post-amplification work are essential to prevent amplicon carryover contamination.
Include positive and no-template negative controls in every run.
limitations: PCR detects nucleic acid presence, which is not always equivalent to viable/infectious organism presence.
Assay-specific analytical sensitivity/specificity and any cross-reactivity are documented in the specific assay's validation, not universal across all PCR assays.
biosafetyNotes: Handle all specimens per standard precautions appropriate to the suspected organism; some pathogen targets require additional biosafety considerations during extraction depending on the organism's risk group.
